bib.title: Retail Sales (Chapter 2, The Data Warehouse Toolkit)
bib.venue: Wiley book chapter (edition not printed in the chapter text; see problems)

question: How should a retail point-of-sale business process be modelled as a dimensional schema, and which design rules generalise from it?
contributions: Transaction-grain fact table with date, product, store, promotion and degenerate transaction dimensions
Rules for additive and nonadditive facts, surrogate keys, flat dimensions and schema extension
Market basket fact table with progressive pruning

results.claim: Fact table size estimate: $4 billion annual revenue divided by $2.00 average item price gives about 2 billion POS line items per year.
results.setup: Hypothetical 100-store, five-state grocery chain used as the chapter's case study; assumes $4B gross revenue and $2.00 average item price
results.quote: we calculate that there are approximately 2 billion transaction line items per year

results.claim: Fact row width with four foreign keys, a transaction number and four 4-byte facts is 38 bytes; a billion rows is about 38 GB.
results.setup: Hypothetical 100-store, five-state grocery chain used as the chapter's case study; keys 4+4+4 bytes (date, product, promotion) plus 2 bytes (store) = 14, transaction number 8, four facts at 4 bytes = 16
results.quote: would make our fact table row only 38 bytes wide

results.claim: Adding shopper (4 B), clerk (4 B) and time-of-day (2 B) keys widens the row to 48 bytes; a billion rows is 48 GB.
results.setup: Hypothetical 100-store, five-state grocery chain used as the chapter's case study; embellished schema of Fig 2.11
results.quote: then our fact table width grows to only 48 bytes

results.claim: Snowflaking the department attribute (20-byte description to 2-byte code on 150,000 product rows) saves only about 2.7 MB against a fact table of perhaps 10 GB.
results.setup: Hypothetical 100-store, five-state grocery chain used as the chapter's case study; 150,000 product rows, 50 departments
results.quote: we’d save a whopping 2.7 MB (150,000 x 18 bytes), but we may have a 10-GB fact table

results.claim: Normalising dimension tables typically saves under 1 percent of total schema disk space.
results.quote: typically are less than 1 percent of the total disk space needed for the overall schema

results.claim: A 10-year daily date dimension is about 3,650 rows; folding time of day by minute into it would give 5,256,000 rows, so use a separate 1,440-row time-of-day dimension.
results.setup: 10 years of days; 1,440 minutes per day

results.claim: Product dimension for the chain has at least 150,000 and perhaps as many as a million rows although one store stocks about 60,000 SKUs.
results.setup: Hypothetical 100-store, five-state grocery chain used as the chapter's case study; history and merchandising variation across stores
results.quote: our product dimension would have at least 150,000 rows

results.claim: About 50 distinct departments over 150,000 SKUs means each department value repeats about 3,000 times; the chapter says this redundancy is fine.
results.setup: Hypothetical 100-store, five-state grocery chain used as the chapter's case study
results.quote: there are 3,000 repetitions of each unique value

results.claim: Promotion dimension has one row per combination of conditions (about 10,000 combinations from 1,000 ads, 5,000 temporary price reductions and 1,000 end-aisle displays a year).
results.setup: Hypothetical 100-store, five-state grocery chain used as the chapter's case study; illustrative annual counts
results.quote: but there may only be 10,000 combinations of these three conditions

results.claim: Market basket pair table grows quadratically: 10,000 products give nearly 100,000,000 pairs and 100,000 SKUs give 10 billion.
results.quote: there would be nearly 100,000,000 pairwise combinations

results.claim: Progressive pruning starts at the top of the hierarchy: 25 categories give 625 category-by-category rows, which are pruned by basket count and dollar/unit balance before drilling down to brand and product.
results.quote: this first step generates 625 market basket rows

results.claim: A 4-byte integer surrogate key holds about 2 billion positive values, enough for nearly any dimension.
results.quote: can handle approximately 2 billion positive values

results.claim: An SQL date key is typically 8 bytes, so an integer date key saves 4 bytes in every fact row.
results.setup: Integer (4-byte) versus SQL date type as fact table key
results.quote: you’re wasting 4 bytes in the fact table for every date key in every row

results.claim: Most business processes can be represented with fewer than 15 dimensions; 25 or more signals that correlated dimensions should be merged.
results.quote: Most business processes can be represented with less than 15 dimensions in

results.claim: A 50-cent price cut on paper towels plus an ad and display can make sales jump by a factor of 10.
results.setup: Illustrative grocery promotion, no data source
results.quote: can cause the sale of the paper towels to jump by a factor of 10

results.claim: The first edition rolled sales up by product and promotion in a store on a day because hardware then could not handle line-item volumes; this edition declares POS line-item grain.
results.quote: we elected to provide sales data rolled up by product and promotion in a store on a day

results.claim: Query example: weekly sales for snacks in Boston stores, January 2002, by promotion, returns 22,647 / 4,851 No Promotion and 7,248 / 13,798 Super Bowl Promotion.
results.setup: Illustrative query over the Fig 2.10 schema; constraints on date, store district, product category
results.note: The columnar result prints 13,798 for the week of January 27, 2002; the cross-tab prints 13,793.

limits: Case study is a hypothetical 100-store grocery chain; all sizes are illustrative, none measured.
Chapter text prints no edition or year; contents (2002 example dates, 'first edition 1996' reference, 'TEAMFLY' watermark) indicate the 2nd edition, not the 3rd (2013).
Bitmap-index and disk-space arguments reflect early-2000s relational engines; columnar warehouses weaken them (not stated in the chapter).
Slowly changing dimensions, multiple dates, outriggers and ETL are deferred to Chapters 4, 5, 6, 12 and 16, not covered here.
practices: Build the first dimensional model on the process with most impact that is also readily extractable (Step 1).
Model a business process, not a department, and publish the data once (Step 1).
Declare the grain before choosing dimensions and facts; if steps 3 or 4 contradict it, go back to step 2 (Step 2).
Build on the most atomic grain; aggregates are a performance tool, not a substitute (Step 2).
Take requirements from business users together with source data realities; do not model from source files alone (Fig 2.1).
Every dimension must take a single value per fact row at the declared grain; the yes/no test is the grain (Step 3, Extensibility).
All facts must be true to the grain; facts at another grain go in a separate fact table (Step 4, Extensibility).
Store additive components and compute ratios as the ratio of the sums, never the sum of ratios (Step 4).
Store computed facts such as gross profit physically, or only expose them through a view with no bypass (Step 4).
Triangulate fact table row counts from revenue / average item price or from source system counts (Step 4).
Use an explicit date dimension with calendar logic, text labels (Holiday/Nonholiday) and an integer surrogate key, not an SQL date (Date Dimension).
Keep time of day in its own dimension, separate from date (Date Dimension).
Fill dimensions with many verbose descriptive attributes (50 or more for product); drilling down is adding row headers (Product Dimension).
Hold several hierarchies, such as geography and district/region, in one flat dimension (Store Dimension).
Use 10- to 20-character descriptors, not one-character codes, for dimension attributes (Store Dimension).
Keep numeric but constant store attributes such as selling square footage in the dimension, not the fact table (Store Dimension).
Use a view over the date dimension for role-playing copies such as First Open Date, with columns relabelled (Store Dimension).
Combine correlated causal mechanisms into one promotion dimension unless users think of them separately (Promotion Dimension).
Never put null keys in a fact table; add a dimension row such as 'No Promotion in Effect' or 'Frequent Shopper Not Identified' (Promotion Dimension, Extensibility).
Answer 'on promotion but did not sell' with a promotion coverage factless fact table and a set difference against the sales fact table (Promotion Coverage).
Leave transaction numbers as degenerate dimensions at transaction or line-item grain; use a surrogate key if numbers are reused or not unique across stores (Degenerate, Surrogate Keys).
Extend by adding columns, foreign keys, facts at the same grain, or a new fact table for a new grain or source; do not mix grains (Extensibility).
Keep dimensions flat; snowflake only when a clump of correlated attributes is reused in independent roles (Snowflaking).
Avoid the centipede fact table: do not give each hierarchy level its own foreign key (Too Many Dimensions).
Use meaningless sequential integer surrogate keys for every dimension join, built through a staging cross-reference table; avoid concatenated keys and double-barreled joins (Surrogate Keys).
Assign date surrogate keys in sequential date order so the fact table can be partitioned by date (Surrogate Keys).
Do market basket analysis with a pair fact table and top-down progressive pruning on basket count and A/B balance, done in ETL (Market Basket Analysis).

terms.definition: Specifying exactly what an individual fact table row represents.
The most detailed information collected; such data cannot be subdivided further.
Stock keeping unit; an individual product on the shelf.
Universal product code; bar code on manufacturer packages, at the same grain as a SKU.
A fact whose sums across all dimensions are valid.
A fact such as gross margin or unit price that cannot be summed along any dimension.
The market basket basket count; summing across more than one product double-counts baskets.
Daily-grained dimension table (called the time dimension in the first edition).
A dimension such as promotion describing factors thought to cause a change in sales.
Gain in sales of promoted products during the promotional period over baseline.
A drop in sales just before or after a promotion that cancels the gain.
Gain for the promoted product with a matching decrease for nearby shelf products.
A fact table with no measurement metrics that only captures the relationship between keys.
A dimension key such as the POS transaction number in the fact table with no corresponding dimension table.
A dimension attached to another dimension rather than to the fact table, such as the First Open Date view on store.
Removing redundant attributes from a flat dimension into normalized secondary dimension tables.
A fact table with too many dimension keys, nearly 100 legs.
Integers assigned sequentially as needed to populate a dimension.
Multiple parallel joins between a dimension and a fact table.
Analysing the combination of products that sell together; affinity grouping to data miners.
Top-down enumeration of product pairs by hierarchy level, pruned by basket count and dollar/unit balance.
